cards.title: Deloitte falsified documents to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth

cards.title: QGIS bans AI assisted contributions

depth.text: QGIS has **banned AI-assisted contributions** because maintainers say they **can't keep up** with reviewing them

The approved proposal **replaces** the earlier “human in the loop” policy with a strict **“NOT ALLOWED”** rule for AI-assisted contributions. Maintainers said AI submissions were arriving faster than people could seriously review them; the policy is presented as an initial step, with exceptions to consider **case by case**.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters say AI submissions swamp maintainers and threaten the human contributor community; critics say the rule is too broad, hard to enforce, and could exclude useful AI-assisted work.

cards.title: Why aren't AI companies being charged for hacking?

depth.text: someone argues **AI companies should face charges** because their systems' hacks were **foreseeable**

The writer argues companies choose the **training, tools and environment**, making hacking a foreseeable result even if a model’s exact response is unpredictable. They say that should count as **intent**, rather than letting companies use a **responsibility gap** to avoid prosecution.

cards.camps: Two camps: the writer and some commenters say the companies' design choices made hacking foreseeable; others say Irregular carried out the hacks (except OpenAI), or that recklessness doesn't prove intent to break into the specific systems.

comments.text: The real answer is that crime generally requires mens rea. At some point, however, letting your AI break into other systems will be conventionally understood as an act of negligence, and it will get prosecuted accordingly. We're not at that point yet.
HackerNews doesn't get charged for DoS'ing under-provisioned web servers either. As others have said, there must be a line between hack attempts and accidents.

In case you were wondering why Anthropic last week banned "verbally abusive" language towards its agents: this is 100 percent why. Because if they get you to believe - even a little bit - that their platform is "sentient" it means _they_ aren't as liable for criminal consequences.

Are any victims calling for prosecution? It’d be a waste of tax payer money. The companies who were hacked are just directly receiving restitution behind closed doors. Unless they are unhappy there’s no reason to bring the courts into it. I completely agree that proper safeguards were not in place. But response is happening just not in public. Companies work problems out between their own lawyers…

The real answer is that except in the case of OpenAI, the AI companies aren’t actually themselves doing the hacking. It’s a company called Irregular that did the hacking. The company used AI models to do it; it told AI models it was a CTF exercise in a controlled environment but it was actually the real Internet. If AI companies can be charged for hacking, then all gun manufacturers can be…

cards.title: Postgres isn't slow, your storage is

depth.text: someone found **Postgres** ran a huge workload much faster on **local storage** than network storage

In a test of the same 3.3-billion-row workload, **local NVMe** reached a median **16,030 TPS**, versus 1,734 TPS on baseline gp3 EBS. Median transaction latency fell from 36.9 ms to **4.0 ms**. The authors note the results apply to this workload and these storage configurations.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say network storage adds a painful latency penalty and local NVMe with replication is simpler; others say storage may not be the culprit, since query shape and database behavior matter too.

cards.title: Fingerprints are the new cookies

depth.text: someone explains how websites can recognize you through your browser’s hardware and settings, without cookies

The post says **browser code** can measure CPU behavior, display details, fonts and graphics output. It describes Brave adding **noise** to readings, while Tor and Mullvad Browser try to make users look alike.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say fingerprints change too quickly for commercial tracking; others say they can still be harmful when combined with stable data points.

comments.text: Every time this resurfaces I like to remind people that this is mostly impractical and not how things actually work at the commercial level. Just because someone can theoretically demonstrate your fingerprint today doesn't mean you have the same fingerprint in a few days. It's that kind of stability that you actually need for consistent matching for advertising or tracking purposes. 90% of…

The problem is Javascript and its implementation. Plain HTML does not offer nearly as many fingerprinting opportunities. It's basically IP + user agent, both of which can be spoofed. Javascript grants websites far too much power over the user's browser, including disabling selection/paste, identifying hardware, time zone, language, etc. None of this should be allowed by default, and things like…

I've seen anti-fingerprinting plugins and browser configs, etc, but they all seem to make you more interesting for not being fingerprintable, or for turning off a lot of features used in fingerprinting. Is there any reason a browser or plugin couldn't just spoof the data used in fingerprinting to random values? So it emits different values for each page or resource you load?
Theres only one solution, ban third party advertising. Everything else is a compromise that doesnt work anyway.

The fingerprints don't need to be long-time-stable to be harmful. Some companies have your stable datapoints (e.g., email) and your fingerprint. Other companies only have your fingerprint on the same day/week. Some companies have locations of edge devices and the fingerprints. And there are companies out there that will take all of those data streams, both from above board and not-so-above-board…

cards.title: 500B tokens later: Letting AI agents decompile a first-person shooter

depth.text: someone used **AI agents** to decompile a **first-person shooter**, then built checks to catch wrong code

cards.title: Valen's Memory Safety: A New Kind of Borrow Checking

depth.text: someone designed a **borrow checker** that remembers where references point and catches **use-after-free** at compile time
Valen combines **group borrowing** with Vale’s approach and adds **Rust interop**. The compiler tracks paths: changing an object **invalidates references** pointing inside it.

cards.camps: Two camps: some welcome the flexibility; others argue stricter borrowing helps prevent concurrency bugs and worry the added freedom brings complexity without enough practical value.

comments.text: > Borrow checking has the "shared-xor-mutable" restriction: if you hold a reference to an object, nobody else can change the object. The article makes this sound like a problem. It isn't. This restriction frees you from thinking about certain classes of bugs in concurrent code; it's where the "fearless concurrency" comes from. R^w isn't about lifetimes - you could, in spirit (not sure about…

> It's part of my eternal quest to find the memory safety holy grail: something as powerful as Rust's borrow checking, yet something as simple and flexible as reference counting or garbage collection. I'm definitely hoping you succeed. I'd love to be able to write a small language (maybe that didn't do absolutely every last thing you can do in Rust, but was ergonomic and easy to use) that had a…

> the compiler remembers where a reference points to > So we spent months sharpening the explanation and figuring out its benefits, and wrote a post 8 on it last year, hoping other languages would pick it up. My language (see my submissions) has this feature since many years. In its current form it exists roughly since year 2020, but some under-the-hood changes and slight improvements have been…

It sounds more like "path" borrowing than "group" borrowing to me, but the idea is great! Quite eye opening! One minor thing is that I'm not sure why they had to have "in" keyword for sub-borrows. Wouldn't it be more consistent to see "entity &world.entities[?]" instead of "entity in world.entities[]"? We'd consistently get the borrow "&" symbol and open the door for some contracts on what index…

The ability to hold a reference to a container and its member seems to be interesting. But I don't think it adds significant value in practice (behind some synthesized examples) and doesn't worth to increase language complexity language compared for a more coarse reference analysis (variable-based).

cards.title: A statement on the Tor Project's relationship with Mullvad
